methods.title: Providing an alternative explanation (cause)
methods.definition: The author provides a different cause/reason for an observed effect, challenging the original cause given.
methods.example:
A: I finally broke the 170 barrier on the LSAT. This was all because I had an awesome tutor.
B: Tutors can only point out the right way to study. Your success on the LSAT is rather due to your incessant hard work.

In this example, A provides a cause/reason for getting over 170 on the LSAT. B, on the other hand, disputes that cause and provides an alternative cause/explanation.

methods.title: Establishing the validity of one explanation (cause) by excluding alternative explanations (causes)
methods.definition: The author narrows down to one specific cause by eliminating other possible explanations (causes).
methods.example:
Gas prices have been increasing recently. Price increases can be caused by increased demand, limited supplies, or unforeseen geopolitical events. Demand and supply have remained constant, so the cause must be due to the war currently going on.

In this example, the author eliminates other possible explanations (causes) (increased demand, limited supplies, unforeseen geopolitical events) to establish the war as the cause of the price increase.

methods.title: Reinterpreting an opponent's evidence so that they are also compatible with an alternative explanation (cause)
methods.definition: The author argues that the evidence given by the opponent can also support a different explanation (cause).
methods.example:
John: I saw Peter the other day, that guy lost over 40 lbs! He must have exercised like crazy this past summer.
David: It's also possible that he just watched his diet really carefully.

In this example, David isn't arguing that Peter didn't exercise. David is simply saying that it is also possible that Peter lost all this weight due to his diet (cause).

methods.title: Infer a causal relationship (cause) from a correlation
methods.definition: The author argues that a correlation between two variables implies a causal relationship (cause).
methods.example:
A positive correlation is a statistical relationship where as one value increases, the other increases as well. As one value decreases, the other value also decreases. For example, as the temperature increases, the amount of sunscreen sold also increases. So we say that there is a correlation between the temperature and sunscreen sales.

Having a correlation between A and B doesn't automatically mean that there is causation (cause) involved between A and B. For instance, there is a positive correlation between how green vegetation is and the number of people going swimming. Are people going swimming because trees are turning green or vice versa? No. There is a common cause for both phenomena, namely that the temperature is rising.

methods.title: Appeal to definition
methods.definition: The author uses a dictionary or textbook definition of a term to support their argument.
methods.example: The author will give a dictionary/textbook definition of a certain term, and go on to argue that the action or event we are discussing fits or doesn't fit this definition.

methods.title: Appeal to authority
methods.definition: The author supports their argument by citing an expert in the field.
methods.example: The author will invoke/appeal to an expert in the field to justify the point they are making.

methods.title: Opponent's policy could have undesirable consequences (causes)
methods.definition: The author argues that following the opponent's recommendation would lead to negative outcomes (causes).
methods.example:
John: Gasoline cars cause a lot of environmental damage, we should ban them outright.
David: But if you ban gasoline cars, how will millions of people survive? Most people need a car to go to work, and if you take away their cars, what will they do?

In this type of reasoning, our author isn't attacking the opponent's reasoning per se, but rather they are suggesting that if we go through with what the opponent is recommending, it can lead to disastrous consequences (causes).

methods.title: Pointing out that the opponent failed to take relevant information into account
methods.definition: The author shows that the opponent's argument overlooks important information.
methods.example:
This pattern of reasoning is very similar to the previous one. The author is offering up additional information/new evidence which will attack/weaken the opponent's argument. It could be that what the opponent is arguing for has undesirable consequences (causes), is impossible to enforce, or difficult to enforce.

John: We should expose the government's corruption. Let's send the evidence to all the major media outlets in the country.
David: You forget that the government owns all the media outlets in our country. Doing so would only endanger yourself.

methods.title: Deriving a general principle from specific examples (causes)
methods.definition: The author formulates a general principle based on specific cases (causes).
methods.example:
A principle is essentially concerned with what you should do, or what should be done. Principles also have applicability to cases not specifically discussed in the stimulus.

"People who break the law should be punished" is a principle. It is applicable regardless of who the person is, or what law was broken.

"All cars must pass the safety standard test before they can be marketed to the public" is also a principle.

"Taylor broke the law, so he should be punished" is NOT a principle. The statement is only talking about one person.

A generalization is very similar. It has applicability to cases not specifically discussed in the stimulus. But a generalization doesn't have to be about what you should do or what should be done. If all the swans I saw were white, and I say "All swans are white", I am making a generalization.

To give a list of examples and to derive a generalization/principle from them is a common pattern of reasoning in Method questions. This pattern of reasoning also appears in other types of questions. Here is an example:

Elon Musk failed many times before he succeeded, so did Steve Jobs, Thomas Edison, and all the great inventors and entrepreneurs that I know about. So in order to be successful, we must learn from our mistakes and never give up (causes).

methods.title: Supporting a conclusion about a specific case by invoking a relevant generalization (cause)
methods.definition: The author uses a generalization (cause) to justify a conclusion about a specific case.
methods.example: Every successful person has overcome many failures in order to be where they are today. So behind Elon Musk's great success story, there must have been countless painful failures (causes).

methods.title: Using a counterexample to attack a general claim
methods.definition: The author provides an example that contradicts the opponent's generalization.
methods.example: The opponent's argument will contain a generalization (this can either be a premise or conclusion). Our author, in response, provides an example which doesn't fit into the opponent's generalization.

methods.title: Attacking an opponent's premise (cause)
methods.definition: The author challenges the foundation (cause) of the opponent's argument.
methods.example: This demonstrates again why when faced with a rebuttal type stimulus, we need to read the opponent's argument carefully, focusing on its structure. Is our author attacking the opponent's premise? If so, then this is the correct answer/method of reasoning.

methods.title: Conclude that members of two groups are likely to share a certain characteristic because of other characteristics they share
methods.definition: The author argues that similarities in some aspects imply similarities in others.
methods.example: The author is basically saying that A and B have one similarity, so they are similar in another aspect. For example: David and John are both from Chicago. David loves deep dish pizza, so John must do so as well.

methods.title: Pointing out that the opponent makes an inappropriate comparison/analogy
methods.definition: The author criticizes the opponent's comparison for being flawed.
methods.example:
Comparable reasoning is again at play here, except this time our author is attacking the comparison made by the opponent. The author is arguing that just because two entities are similar in one aspect, it doesn't mean they are similar in another aspect.

Continuing with the example above, we can argue that just because two people are from the same city, it doesn't mean they will like the same food.

methods.title: Using an analogy to advance one's argument
methods.definition: The author uses an analogy to clarify or support their point.
methods.example: An analogy is, according to the dictionary definition, "a comparison between two things, typically for the purpose of clarification." In other words, it is an advanced form of a comparison. For instance, physicists have used the analogy of a gun shooting bullets to better describe the process of radiation, where energy is "shot" out in the form of particles. The two processes are similar enough so that we can visualize one to better understand the other.

methods.title: Pointing out an erroneous assumption in the opponent's argument (cause)
methods.definition: The author identifies a flawed assumption in the opponent's reasoning (cause).
methods.example:
An assumption is essentially an implicit/unstated premise (cause). It is something that would fill in the reasoning gap between the premise and conclusion, but which, for some reason, has been left out by the author.

Take a look at the following argument:
All JDs must have taken the LSAT, so John must have taken the LSAT.

We have a premise (JD → LSAT) and a conclusion (John must have taken the LSAT), but clearly something is missing. We need an additional piece of information to make the argument complete:

John is a JD candidate/degree holder.

This piece of missing information is the assumption (cause). The whole argument, in its complete form, is like this:

All JDs must have taken the LSAT (premise), John is a JD candidate (assumption), so John must have taken the LSAT (conclusion).

In Method questions, arguments will sometimes contain assumptions (causes). Both the opponent's argument and/or the author's argument can contain these assumptions. They are hard to spot because they don't appear in the stimulus. We have to understand the argument and find the gap between premise and conclusion, finally inferring the assumptions (causes) ourselves.

An especially tricky format is when the opponent's argument contains an assumption (cause), and our author is attacking that assumption, rather than the opponent's premise or conclusion. When faced with such a reasoning pattern, many students will be at a loss of what to do, as what the author is saying seems to have no connection to what the opponent was saying. Continuing with the same example, the stimulus would look something like this:

Peter: All JDs must have taken the LSAT, so John must have taken the LSAT.
David: But John isn't a JD, he's an LLM.

Here, David is directly contradicting Peter's assumption that John has a JD. When looking at harder Method questions, make sure to ask yourself if any of the arguments contain assumptions (causes).

methods.title: Showing that the opponent's conclusion, if true, leads to an impossible/unlikely result (cause)
methods.definition: The author demonstrates that the opponent's conclusion leads to an absurd outcome (cause).
methods.example:
This type of reasoning looks very similar to the conditional reasoning contrapositive. Remember that in a conditional relationship, A → B, its contrapositive is B → A.

In this type of argument, the opponent will come to the conclusion A. Our author, on the other hand, will state that if conclusion A is true, it will lead to/likely lead to B. However, since B is not true, A cannot be true either. Here is an example:

John: The taller you are, the better you are as a basketball player. (A)
David: If that were true, the world's tallest person would be the best basketball player in the world. (If A were true, it leads to B)

Here, David's assumption (cause) is that the tallest person in the world is NOT also the best basketball player. Hence, John is mistaken in his belief about the correlation between height and basketball skills. (B is not the case, hence A is wrong as well. B → A)
